title: Judges 18:11–26
context: Six hundred armed Danites march north, stop at Micah’s house, and take his image, ephod, teraphim, and priest. The Levite gladly accepts promotion to priest of a tribe. When Micah pursues, the Danites threaten him and he turns back powerless. The scene shows idolatry, theft, and intimidation feeding one another.

verses.text: The family of the Danites set out from Zorah and Eshtaol with six hundred men armed with weapons of war.
verses.arminianNotes: Six hundred armed men set out from Zorah and Eshtaol. Arminian readers note the scale of the move and how the tribe’s decision rests on the spies’ report and an uncertain oracle.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the number as a small force for a tribal migration, reflecting Dan’s weakness. The march begins without any mention of seeking the LORD at Shiloh.

verses.text: They went up and encamped in Kiriath Jearim in Judah. Therefore they call that place Mahaneh Dan to this day. Behold, it is behind Kiriath Jearim.
verses.arminianNotes: The Danites camp near Kiriath Jearim in Judah, giving the place the name Mahaneh Dan, camp of Dan. Arminian readers note how the narrator links names to events, preserving memory for later readers.
verses.reformedNotes: The phrase to this day shows the narrator writing for later readers who knew the place. Reformed readers note that the name preserves the memory of Dan’s journey, though the exact site is not certain.

verses.text: They passed from there to the hill country of Ephraim, and came to the house of Micah.
verses.arminianNotes: The army reaches Micah’s house in the hill country of Ephraim. Arminian readers note that the Danites now return with intent, not curiosity: what the spies saw on their first visit has become a target, showing how a casual glance at idolatry can grow into a plan.
verses.reformedNotes: The route brings the Danites back to the house where their spies received the oracle. Reformed readers note the grim logic: the shrine where they sought guidance is about to be plundered, exposing how little reverence the tribe has for what it treats as sacred.

verses.text: Then the five men who went to spy out the country of Laish answered and said to their brothers, “Do you know that there is in these houses an ephod, and teraphim, and a carved image, and a molten image? Now therefore consider what you have to do.”
verses.arminianNotes: The spies tell their brothers about the ephod, teraphim, carved image, and molten image, and ask what they should do. Arminian readers note that the spies themselves suggest the theft, revealing their regard for the objects as useful tools.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the objects valued for their supposed power rather than rejected as idols. The question consider what you have to do invites the tribe into a planned robbery. The WEB footnote again explains teraphim as household idols.

verses.text: They went over there and came to the house of the young Levite man, even to the house of Micah, and asked him how he was doing.
verses.arminianNotes: The Danites greet the young Levite and ask how he is doing. Arminian readers see friendly words masking a plan to take what belongs to his employer, a reminder that warmth can be used to disarm a conscience before asking it to compromise.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the polite greeting that precedes the theft. The narrator lets outward courtesy and hidden intent sit side by side, a pattern of deception that runs through the story from Micah’s first theft onward.

verses.text: The six hundred men armed with their weapons of war, who were of the children of Dan, stood by the entrance of the gate.
verses.arminianNotes: Six hundred armed men wait by the entrance of the gate. For Arminian readers the show of force removes any real choice from Micah’s household, turning what follows into intimidation rather than negotiation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the armed men as a picture of power taking whatever it wants, exactly the anarchy described by the refrain of 18:1, with no king or judge to restrain the strong.

verses.text: The five men who went to spy out the land went up, and came in there, and took the engraved image, the ephod, the teraphim, and the molten image; and the priest stood by the entrance of the gate with the six hundred men armed with weapons of war.
verses.arminianNotes: While the priest stands with the soldiers, the five spies empty the shrine. Arminian interpreters observe that the priest’s position is already compromised: he is physically with the raiders before he formally joins them.
verses.reformedNotes: The full list of objects is repeated, emphasizing that nothing of Micah’s shrine is left. Reformed readers note that the narrator lingers on the inventory to show how thoroughly the gods Micah trusted can be carried away by men.

verses.text: When these went into Micah’s house, and took the engraved image, the ephod, the teraphim, and the molten image, the priest said to them, “What are you doing?”
verses.arminianNotes: The priest asks, What are you doing? His protest is brief and quickly silenced. Arminian readers see a loyalty to Micah that was always thin, resting on wages rather than on conviction about what was right before God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the only objection raised carries no appeal to God, law, or covenant. The priest’s concern is practical rather than spiritual, which fits a ministry that began as a hired arrangement.

verses.text: They said to him, “Hold your peace, put your hand on your mouth, and go with us. Be a father and a priest to us. Is it better for you to be priest to the house of one man, or to be priest to a tribe and a family in Israel?”
verses.arminianNotes: The Danites tell the priest to keep quiet and offer him a larger congregation. Arminian readers see temptation by ambition, an appeal to status that the Levite does not resist.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the argument: a tribe is better than one household. The offer measures ministry by size and prestige rather than faithfulness, a temptation recognizable in many ages.

verses.text: The priest’s heart was glad, and he took the ephod, the teraphim, and the engraved image, and went with the people.
verses.arminianNotes: The priest’s heart was glad, and he took the objects and went with them. Arminian readers see a man whose choices are driven by advancement rather than conviction, a sober warning for those in ministry.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the Levite himself carries off his employer’s idols. The narrator shows betrayal and theft by the one entrusted with religious care.

verses.text: So they turned and departed, and put the little ones, the livestock, and the goods before them.
verses.arminianNotes: The Danites place their little ones, livestock, and goods in front of them as they leave. Arminian readers note the practical concern to protect the vulnerable, a detail that also shows the tribe expected Micah to pursue them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the arrangement as a military precaution that puts the fighting men at the rear. The verse makes clear that this is a whole migration of households, not merely a raid by soldiers.

verses.text: When they were a good way from the house of Micah, the men who were in the houses near Micah’s house gathered together and overtook the children of Dan.
verses.arminianNotes: Micah’s neighbors gather and overtake the Danites at some distance from his house. Arminian readers note that Micah can rally a little local support, but it is small and unprepared against a tribe on the move.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the pursuit as the natural response of people who have been robbed. Yet the scene underscores Micah’s helplessness now that the gods and the priest he relied on are gone.

verses.text: As they called to the children of Dan, they turned their faces, and said to Micah, “What ails you, that you come with such a company?”
verses.arminianNotes: The Danites turn and ask Micah what ails him. Arminian readers hear mocking innocence in the question, as if the thieves had done nothing wrong and the victim were the one causing trouble.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note how power redefines wrongdoing: the victim is treated as the aggressor. The exchange illustrates the moral confusion of a time when there was no just authority to name theft for what it was.

verses.text: He said, “You have taken away my gods which I made, and the priest, and have gone away! What more do I have? How can you ask me, ‘What ails you?’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Micah cries that they have taken the gods he made, and asks what he has left. Arminian readers see the tragic emptiness of idolatry: gods that can be stolen cannot protect their maker.
verses.reformedNotes: The phrase my gods which I made exposes the folly that prophets later mock (Isaiah 44:9-20). Reformed readers see in Micah’s lament the bankruptcy of worship directed to what human hands produce.

verses.text: The children of Dan said to him, “Don’t let your voice be heard among us, lest angry fellows fall on you, and you lose your life, with the lives of your household.”
verses.arminianNotes: The Danites threaten Micah with violence if he speaks further. Arminian readers note how force silences justice when there is no authority to restrain it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the threat as the logic of a society where everyone does what is right in his own eyes. Might, not right, decides the outcome.

verses.text: The children of Dan went their way; and when Micah saw that they were too strong for him, he turned and went back to his house.
verses.arminianNotes: Micah sees that the Danites are too strong for him and turns back home. Arminian readers note the quiet end of his religious project, lost to stronger men with the same disregard for God’s law.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Micah, who once stole from his mother, now loses what he made to thieves. The narrator lets the irony speak without comment.
